newsitem.title: UK: UK primary fuel demand fell 6.9 percent in Q1 1997.
newsitem.headline: UK primary fuel demand fell 6.9 percent in Q1 1997.

text.p: British primary fuels demand fell by 6.9 percent in the first quarter of 1997 to 63.6 million tonnes of oil equivalent as lower consumption of coal, natural gas and petroleum products offset rising use of primary electricity, the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) said Tuesday.

Consumption of coal, natural gas and petroleum fell by 14.2 percent, 9.4 percent and 3.1 percent respectively, while primary electricity consumption increased by 9.5 per cent, according to provisional figures released by the DTI.
First quarter oil demand, including non-energy use, fell by 3.6 percent to 20.4 million tonnes, largely because of a 15.7 percent fall in fuel oil deliveries.

Gasoline demand was virtually unchanged but unleaded petrol continued to increase its market share, accounting for 70.8 percent of first quarter deliveries, up from 67.1 percent in the same period last year.
Diesel fuel deliveries increased by 4.6 percent, the DTI said.
Petrol and diesel pump prices were about 10 percent higher than in the first quarter of 1996, despite a penny per litre fall between mid-February and mid-March.
"These falls reflect lower crude oil prices and ongoing competition in the retail market particularly from supermarket chains," the DTI said.
Benchmark Brent crude oil fell from $24.61 a barrel on January 2 to $19.20 on March 31, losing 22 percent of its value in three months.
Primary fuels production was broadly steady, rising a modest 0.4 percent to 78.1 million tonnes of oil equivalent in the first quarter.

Oil production rose by 2.6 percent while primary electricity production jumped 10.7 percent, largely due to improved performance from Magnox nuclear power stations where a large number of reactors were unavailable a year earlier.
